title: Avimi (a leading Babylonian amora of the second generation)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman writes that who his teachers and forebears were is nowhere recorded; all that we know is that he was Rav Chisda’s teacher, as in Menachot 7a, where Rav Chisda said, "I received good beatings from Avimi". Likewise we find "Rav Chisda said Avimi" in Sukkah 16b, Ketubot 71b and 100b, Gittin 26b, Sotah 9a, Bava Kamma 13b, Sanhedrin 46a and 81b, Zevachim 26a and 27a, Menachot 77b, Bekhorot 44a; and Rav Chisda raised a difficulty against him in Avodah Zarah 14b.

Hyman also finds "Mar Yehuda said Avimi" in Chullin 48a (so it should read in Eruvin 24a as well, where "Rav Yehuda" appears by error, according to Dikdukei Soferim); and in Shabbat 57b, "Rav Yehuda in the name of Abaye," it seems it should read "Mar Yehuda in the name of Avimi." Likewise Ulla bar Menashya spoke in his name in Gittin 79a.

It appears to Hyman that in his old age, or having fallen ill and forgotten his learning, he went to his student Rav Chisda to recover his learning, as in Menachot 7a, and encountered Rav Nachman and engaged in discussion with him; and in Bava Kamma 12a Rav Nachman said to Rava, "Avimi taught" (so too mentioned in Eruvin 58b, Moed Katan 5b), and in Nedarim 47a, "Avimi inquired" — but there it should read "Abaye inquired," as in the reading of the Rosh, since afterward Rava said, "Come, hear."[^1][^2][^3]

notes.text: Menachot7a explicitly identifies Avimi as Rav Chisda’s teacher and says Avimi went to Rav Chisda after forgetting his learning. The good beatings phrase is retained as a scholarly idiom; it alone does not establish a biographical account of physical punishment.
The Mar Yehuda / Rav Yehuda and Avimi / Abaye changes are Hyman’s proposed readings. His alternatives of old age or illness are preserved.

The heading identifies this Avimi as one of the leading Babylonian amoraim of the second generation, distinguishing the article from Hyman’s short Avimi name index. In the named William Davidson Menachot 7a text, Rav Chisda recalls learning from Avimi; Avimi later goes to Rav Chisda to recover forgotten learning, and the next paragraph explicitly names Rav Nachman. The teacher and visitor directions are preserved. Hyman’s explanation by old age or illness, his statement about unknown teachers and forebears, and his proposed Mar Yehuda/Rav Yehuda and Avimi/Abaye readings remain his claims.
